rows.subtype: Stage 1: The bully picks a target [Actor]
rows.description: A child who feels powerless at home or wants status notices a quieter classmate who does not fight back. Picking the target is often about the bully's need for power and admiration, not about anything the target did.
He starts with a nickname, a nudge or hiding a bag, and watches for reaction and audience. If nobody stops him and others laugh, he learns that cruelty pays and moves to more.

rows.subtype: Stage 3: The target's confusion and shame [Receiver]
rows.description: The child feels stomach aches before school, thinks it is his fault and hides it from parents for fear of making things worse. Fear and shame make bullying secret, which helps it continue.
Classmates feel sorry but fear being next, some laugh to stay safe, and a few even join. Each waits for someone else to act, so a group of kind children can still allow harm.

rows.subtype: Stage 5: An ally breaks the silence [Response]
rows.description: One child sits beside the target, says "come play with us" and tells a teacher afterwards. Standing with the target, and telling an adult, is not tale-telling; it is safe and brave, and it changes the group's mood.

rows.subtype: Stage 6: Adults act on both sides [Response]
rows.description: The school protects the target, is firm with the bully and also asks what unmet need drives him. The child who bullied needs consequence and support to learn other ways of getting respect.
A five-year-old is refused a second sweet and feels the world unfair. Her body reacts before her words, with shouting "I hate you" and stamping.
She tries crying, promising and finally shouting, watching whether the limit will move. If it moves after a tantrum, she learns that tantrums work, and the pattern grows stronger.
The parent, tired after work, feels stung by "I hate you" and is tempted to punish or match the child's volume. Noticing his own heat and taking a breath first is the key moment.
He says "I hear you are angry. The answer is still no more sweets today." He does not shame her, bargain or shout, and stays available for comfort.
After crying she climbs into his lap, ashamed and relieved. The child needs to know that anger did not break the bond, and any harsh words did not make her unlovable.

Later they talk through what to do when angry, such as stomping softly, drawing or asking for a hug. The parent may also apologise for raised voice, modelling repair and teaching that everyone can make things right.

A teacher notices a quiet student's careful questions in science and offers extra reading. Being noticed by an adult who is neither parent nor friend can feel surprising, and quietly powerful, to the teen.

The student turns up at the teacher's desk after school with doubts about becoming a doctor. She tests whether the teacher will take her seriously or laugh, and each respectful reply lowers her guard.
She copies his phrases and treats his opinions as the truth. Admiration is a real motor of growth, though it can hide the mentor's limits and the student's own judgement.

The teacher critiques her project bluntly, and she feels stung and briefly angry. A good mentor holds high standards with warmth, and the student learns that criticism from someone who cares is a gift.
She chooses a different stream than he advised and fears his disappointment. A wise mentor says "I would have chosen otherwise, but I trust your reasons," and the bond becomes more equal.

rows.subtype: Stage 6: Boundaries and a lasting thread [Response]
rows.description: The mentor keeps relations professional and open, with others aware, so the guidance stays safe. Any adult who asks for secrecy, gifts or private contact beyond the role should prompt the teen to tell a parent or other trusted adult.
